summary: Young children (around ages 5–6) learn direction and turning as a doing skill: physically moving forward/backward and turning their whole body through whole, half, quarter and three-quarter turns, then both following and giving route directions. The core insight is that a turn is an amount of rotation about a fixed spot — felt in the body — distinct from travelling a distance. Main hurdles are confusing turning with moving, under-/over-rotating when there is no target to turn toward, and left/right (which is frame-dependent and matures later). Embodied whole-body movement is the primary teaching medium; a programmable floor-robot or route game is proposed as a companion that can show the result of a turn immediately (a wrong turn visibly misses the goal), though its relative teaching value over embodied movement is not established.
misconceptions: Confusing a turn (rotation on the spot) with moving forward — 'turning' by walking in a curve or stepping sideways
Under- or over-rotating: a 'quarter turn' that is a random amount because it is not referenced to a target facing
Left/right reversed, especially relative to the direction of travel or a facing partner (frame-dependence)
Treating half or quarter of a turn as unrelated to half or quarter of anything else — no sense of a fractional turn amount

activities.title: Turn your whole body on the spot
steps: Stand on a marked spot (hoop or footprints) with both feet staying put throughout the turn.
Mark your start facing (e.g. 'I'm facing the door'), then make a quarter turn to your right and name your new facing ('now the window').

Go back to your start facing (the door). Make a half turn and check you are facing the opposite way from the start; go back to the start facing, make a whole turn and check you are facing the same way as the start.

Go back to your start facing, then make a three-quarter turn to your right and check where you now face (three quarter-turns to the right from the start, the same facing as one quarter turn to the left).
Make two quarter turns in a row in the same direction (both to the right) and compare: is that the same as one half turn?
activities.insight: A turn is an amount of rotation about a fixed point, felt in the body — not travelling. A quarter turn lands you on a new facing (about 90° from the start), a half turn faces you the opposite way, a three-quarter turn is three quarter-turns on, and a whole turn returns you to the same facing.

activities.title: Give and follow a route
steps: Follow a spoken route given by an adult or partner: 'go forward two, turn left a quarter, go forward one.'
Then GIVE directions yourself: describe how to walk from here to the bookshelf as a sequence of moves and turns.
Have your listener walk your exact words — if they miss the bookshelf or hit a wall, find the missing or wrong move or turn and re-give the route.
Try describing the route for walking backward from the bookshelf to the start.
activities.insight: A followable route is a coordinated sequence of moves AND turns with correct directional words — leaving out the turns breaks the path. Giving a route (not just following one) shows the directional words have become a productive tool.

activities.title: Program a robot along a floor grid (companion)
steps: On a floor grid or maze, string commands for a character/robot: 'forward 2', 'turn left a quarter', 'forward 1'.
Aim the robot at a goal; if a turn is the wrong direction or amount, the robot faces the wrong way and misses or runs into a wall.
Watch the start and finish facings shown as an arrow, and adjust so a quarter turn visibly lands the arrow 90° on.
Compare turning-then-walking with walking-then-turning and notice the different results.
activities.insight: A 'quarter turn' only makes sense as landing on a new facing toward the next target, and the order of turning and walking matters: turn-then-walk is different from walk-then-turn.

checkQuestion: Set the task and watch: 'Stand on this spot facing the door. Make a quarter turn to your right. ... Now make a half turn. ... Now give me directions to walk from here to the bookshelf.' Watch the body rotation and listen to the route — do not ask them to explain the procedure.
checkAnswer: Rotates on the spot without walking; a quarter turn lands them facing 90° from the start (toward the next target) and a half turn faces them the opposite way; and their route directions are a followable sequence of moves and turns with correct directional words.
